# Developing FinTech adoption capability among Thai Gen Z finance students: Influencing AI literacy, self-directed learning and innovative thinking skill

## ARTICLE INFO ABSTRACT

### _Keywords:_ This study investigates the effect of AI literacy on FinTech adoption capability, while examining 

AI literacy the mediating roles of self-directed learning and innovative thinking skills among Generation Z Self-directed learning finance students in Thailand. A quantitative research approach was employed, with data collected Innovative thinking skill

via an online questionnaire administered to 391 undergraduate finance students. The data were 

FinTech adoption capability Generation Z students analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The results reveal 

that AI literacy has significant positive effects on self-directed learning, innovative thinking skills, and FinTech adoption capability. Although self-directed learning does not directly influence FinTech adoption capability, it exhibits a significant indirect effect through innovative thinking skills. Further mediation analysis indicates that innovative thinking skills function as a critical mechanism through which AI literacy and self-directed learning contribute to effective FinTech adoption. These findings suggest that enhancing AI literacy alone may not be sufficient unless it is complemented by the development of self-directed learning behaviors and innovative thinking skills. This study contributes to the growing body of literature on financial technology adoption within educational settings and offers policy-relevant insights for strengthening the digital 

competencies of finance students in the context of ongoing digital transformation.

## 1. Introduction

In an era where digital technologies are rapidly transforming the global landscape, the financial industry has undergone profound changes driven by technological advancements, particularly through the rapid expansion of financial technology (FinTech). FinTech has fundamentally reshaped the delivery of financial services, encompassing mobile banking applications, e-wallet transactions, and digital asset investments, thereby reflecting the broader wave of digital disruption that compels organizations to adapt at an accel- erated pace (Gumilar et al., 2024; Sibanda et al., 2020). In Thailand, where digital economy policies have been actively promoted, the

All rights are reserved, including those for text and data mining, AI training, and similar technologies. financial sector has become one of the most dynamic adopters of digital innovations. At the same time, the emergence of Generation Z—a cohort raised in an environment deeply embedded with information technology and social media—has further accelerated this transformation. Generation Z is widely recognized for its high level of digital proficiency and stronger inclination to adopt emerging technologies compared to previous generations (Ratanabanchuen, 2021). Accordingly, Generation Z finance students constitute a particularly relevant group for investigation, as they are not only active users of FinTech in their daily lives but also future financial professionals who will be required to work extensively with artificial intelligence (AI) and other digital technologies in their careers (Srivastava et al., 2024).

Although prior research has emphasized the importance of AI literacy as a critical factor enabling individuals to effectively utilize financial technologies (Imjai et al., 2025), systematic examination of AI-related knowledge within the academic training and practical learning of finance students in Thailand remains limited. Furthermore, a persistent issue within the Thai education system is the underdevelopment of self-directed learning skills, which are essential for enabling learners to independently manage and advance their learning without excessive reliance on external guidance (Wu & Lin, 2009). The capacity for self-directed learning is likely to play a pivotal role in helping students continuously adapt to the rapidly evolving FinTech landscape. In addition, innovative thinking skills are equally important in preparing finance students for future professional environments. Such skills emphasize creative ideation, novel problem-solving, and calculated risk-taking, all of which are increasingly required in technology-driven financial contexts ([Affandy et al., 2024)](#credit-authorship-contribution-statement). When finance students possess strong AI literacy in conjunction with self-directed learning capabilities and innovative thinking skills, they are better positioned to adapt effectively and leverage evolving financial technologies in meaningful ways ([Ding et al., 2024)](#credit-authorship-contribution-statement). Therefore, this study seeks to examine how AI literacy influences FinTech adoption capability among Generation Z finance students, while incorporating the mediating roles of self-directed learning and innovative thinking skills. These constructs represent critical competencies in the digital economy and are consistent with prior research highlighting their influence on technology adoption behaviors.

This study contributes not only to advancing the theoretical understanding of the role of AI literacy in FinTech adoption within educational contexts but also provides practical insights for curriculum development and instructional design that emphasize the cultivation of self-directed learning and innovative thinking among finance students. The findings offer valuable implications for academics, educators, and higher education institutions aiming to align teaching practices with evolving labor market demands and technological advancements (Stolpe & Hallstrom, 2024¨ ). Moreover, by focusing on Generation Z finance students in Thailand, this research provides deeper insights into the technological perceptions and behaviors of younger cohorts, which may inform financial institutions and businesses in designing FinTech products, services, and marketing strategies that effectively address the needs and expectations of emerging users (Thanapongporn et al., 2024). Overall, this study holds both theoretical and practical significance in elucidating how AI literacy, self-directed learning, and innovative thinking skills collectively enhance FinTech adoption capability among Generation Z finance students in Thailand, thereby contributing to the sustainable development of future financial pro- fessionals in the digital economy.

## 2. Literature review

### _2.1._ _Theoretical foundation_

This study is grounded in an integrative theoretical framework that combines Social Cognitive Theory (SCT), Self-Directed Learning Theory, and the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) to explain the development of FinTech capability in the digital economy. Within this framework, Social Cognitive Theory serves as the overarching perspective, emphasizing the dynamic interplay among personal factors, cognitive processes, and behavioral outcomes ([Bandura, 1991)](#credit-authorship-contribution-statement). From this standpoint, AI literacy is conceptualized as a critical personal capability that shapes individuals’ ability to interpret, evaluate, and effectively utilize digital technologies. It enhances not only technical knowledge but also cognitive readiness to engage with complex and evolving technological environments. Building on this foundation, Self-Directed Learning Theory explains the mechanisms through which individuals transform foun- dational knowledge into higher-order competencies. Self-directed learning reflects an individual's capacity to set learning goals, regulate learning strategies, and independently evaluate learning outcomes (Garrison, 1997a, 1997b; Knowles, 1975). In this study, AI literacy is posited to facilitate self-directed learning behaviors, enabling individuals to continuously adapt and acquire new knowledge within rapidly changing digital contexts. Furthermore, innovative thinking skills represent a higher-order cognitive outcome char- acterized by the ability to generate novel ideas, think flexibly, and solve problems under conditions of uncertainty (Runco & Jaeger, 2012; Scott et al., 2004). Within the SCT framework, innovative thinking can be viewed as a cognitive transformation process that emerges from self-directed learning and mediates the relationship between knowledge acquisition and the development of practical capabilities.

With regard to the outcome variable, this study draws on the Technology Acceptance Model, which traditionally explains tech- nology adoption through perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use ([Davis, 1989)](#credit-authorship-contribution-statement). However, this study extends TAM by conceptualizing FinTech adoption capability as a more advanced form of technology engagement, encompassing not only adoption intention but also actual usage, knowledge application, and the ability to evaluate issues such as security and trustworthiness. This extension reflects a shift from perception-based adoption toward capability-based outcomes. In addition to this, the proposed framework suggests a process-oriented mechanism in which AI literacy, as a personal capability, influences self-directed learning as a learning process, which in turn fosters innovative thinking as a form of cognitive transformation, ultimately leading to FinTech adoption capability as a behavioral and skill-based outcome. By integrating these theoretical perspectives, this study provides a coherent and unified explanation of how foundational digital competencies are translated into practical technological capabilities. In 

doing so, it addresses a key limitation in prior research, which has largely overlooked the roles of learning processes and cognitive development in shaping technology adoption.

### _2.2._ _AI literacy_

AI literacy in this study is conceptualized as a foundational technological competence that enables individuals to understand, evaluate, and appropriately apply artificial intelligence (AI) in both learning and financial contexts. Rather than being treated as a higher-order cognitive outcome, AI literacy is positioned as a domain-specific capability that precedes and facilitates subsequent learning and cognitive transformation processes. This conceptualization is grounded in Social Cognitive Theory (SCT), which posits that knowledge structures shape individuals' cognitive processing and behavioral responses in complex environments ([Bandura, 1991)](#credit-authorship-contribution-statement). From this perspective, AI literacy represents a key personal capability that facilitates individuals’ interaction with AI-driven systems and supports subsequent learning and decision-making processes.

Consistent with prior literature, AI literacy encompasses an understanding of core AI concepts, including algorithmic mechanisms, machine learning processes, and big data utilization, as well as awareness of ethical considerations and societal implications ([Chiu et al., 2024;](#credit-authorship-contribution-statement) Long & Magerko, 2020). However, in contrast to perspectives that implicitly position AI literacy as an advanced cognitive capability, this study explicitly distinguishes AI literacy from higher-order constructs by framing it as an input capability that enables, rather than reflects, cognitive transformation. This distinction is particularly important given the conceptual proximity among AI literacy, self-directed learning, and innovative thinking identified in prior research.

Operationally, AI literacy comprises five dimensions: (1) AI conceptual understanding (Sarker, 2022); (2) AI technical awareness (Sarker, 2022); (3) ethical consideration (Long & Magerko, 2020); (4) AI application proficiency ([Ali et al., 2024)](#credit-authorship-contribution-statement); and (5) AI communication skills ([Chiu et al., 2024)](#credit-authorship-contribution-statement). Collectively, these dimensions capture individuals' practical competence in using AI without conflating it with higher-order cognitive transformation processes. Within the proposed framework, and consistent with SCT, AI lit- eracy is expected to influence self-directed learning by enhancing individuals’ perceived capability to regulate their own learning processes. Individuals with stronger AI-related knowledge are better positioned to identify learning needs, evaluate information sources, and adapt learning strategies in technology-rich environments (Garrison, 1997a, 1997b; Knowles, 1975). Furthermore, AI literacy is expected to influence innovative thinking skills through its role in shaping cognitive processes. Exposure to AI systems and their underlying logic provides informational and analytical resources that support idea generation, problem reframing, and flexible thinking ([Broekhuizen et al., 2023)](#credit-authorship-contribution-statement). In line with SCT, this reflects the transformation of knowledge into higher-order cognitive out- comes through learning processes, rather than implying a direct equivalence between AI literacy and innovation. Finally, AI literacy is expected to exert a direct effect on FinTech adoption capability. Individuals with stronger AI-related knowledge are better able to evaluate the functionality, risks, and reliability of AI-driven financial technologies (Pinski & Benlian, 2024). Moving beyond perception-based approaches, this study conceptualizes FinTech adoption capability as a skill-based outcome encompassing knowledge of FinTech tools, frequency of use, and awareness of security and trust considerations. Accordingly, AI literacy is theorized as a foundational input capability that drives learning mechanisms and cognitive transformation processes, ul- timately leading to FinTech adoption capability. Based on this theoretical rationale, the following hypotheses are proposed: 

| **H1**. | AI literacy has a positive effect on self-directed learning. |
| --- | --- |
| **H2**. | AI literacy has a positive effect on innovative thinking skill. |
| **H3**. | AI literacy has a positive effect on FinTech adoption capability |
| _2.3._ | _Self-directed learning_ |

Self-directed learning (SDL) in this study is conceptualized as a self-regulatory learning mechanism through which individuals actively plan, monitor, and evaluate their own learning processes, rather than as a general cognitive ability or outcome. This definition is grounded in both Self-Directed Learning Theory and Social Cognitive Theory (SCT), which emphasize that learning behavior is shaped by individuals’ capacity to regulate their cognition, motivation, and actions in response to environmental demands ([Bandura, 1991;](#credit-authorship-contribution-statement) Garrison, 1997a, 1997b; Knowles, 1975). From this perspective, SDL represents a process-oriented capability that governs how individuals transform knowledge into meaningful learning outcomes.

In contrast to AI literacy, which reflects domain-specific technological competence, SDL focuses on the regulation of learning processes, including goal setting, strategic planning, self-monitoring, and the adaptive adjustment of learning strategies ([Aladini et al., 2025)](#credit-authorship-contribution-statement). This distinction is essential to avoid conceptual overlap, as SDL does not capture what individuals know or produce, but rather how they manage and direct their own learning activities. By positioning SDL as a learning mechanism, this study clearly differentiates it from AI literacy (input capability) and innovative thinking skills (cognitive transformation outcomes).

From an indicator-based perspective, SDL comprises four key dimensions: (1) goal setting, referring to the ability to define clear and contextually relevant learning objectives (Garrison, 1997a, 1997b); (2) self-monitoring, involving the continuous evaluation of one's learning progress and understanding (Li et al., 2023); (3) self-motivation, reflecting intrinsic motivation to engage in learning without reliance on external incentives (Garrison, 1997a, 1997b); and (4) resource utilization, defined as the ability to identify and effectively leverage learning resources, including digital tools and expert networks (Finn et al., 2024). These dimensions capture regulatory processes rather than knowledge or creative outputs, thereby reinforcing SDL's role as a mechanism rather than an outcome construct. Within the proposed framework, SDL is expected to influence innovative thinking skills by enabling individuals to engage more 

deeply with knowledge, experiment with alternative solutions, and iteratively refine their understanding. From an SCT perspective, self-regulated learners are more likely to engage in reflective thinking and adaptive problem-solving, which are essential for generating novel and useful ideas ([Bandura, 1991)](#credit-authorship-contribution-statement). Accordingly, innovative thinking is conceptualized as a cognitive outcome that emerges from regulated learning processes, rather than as a direct extension of knowledge acquisition. Additionally, SDL is expected to influence FinTech adoption capability, as individuals who effectively regulate their own learning are better equipped to independently explore, practice, and evaluate new technologies in dynamic environments. In contrast to traditional technology adoption models that emphasize perceptions such as usefulness or ease of use, SDL reflects the behavioral capacity to continuously learn and adapt to evolving technological systems—an ability that is particularly critical in FinTech contexts characterized by rapid innovation. This process-oriented perspective also explains why SDL is modeled as a mediator in this study, rather than alternative constructs such as trust or perceived risk, which primarily capture evaluative judgments rather than learning-driven capability development. Given that, SDL is positioned as a central learning mechanism that transforms foundational knowledge into higher-order cognitive and behavioral outcomes within the proposed process-based framework. Based on these theoretical arguments, the following hypotheses are proposed: 

**H4**. Self-directed learning has a positive effect on innovative thinking skill.

**H5**. Self-directed learning has a positive effect on FinTech adoption capability.

### _2.4._ _Innovative thinking skill_

Innovative thinking skill (ITS) in this study is conceptualized as an advanced cognitive outcome that reflects an individual's ca- pacity to generate original ideas, reconceptualize problems, and apply flexible reasoning in complex and uncertain environments. Rather than representing a basic form of knowledge or a learning process, ITS is positioned as a higher-order cognitive capability that emerges from prior learning experiences. This conceptualization is grounded in both creativity research and Social Cognitive Theory (SCT), which posit that higher-order cognitive outcomes develop through iterative learning, self-regulation, and continuous inter- action with environmental stimuli ([Bandura, 1991;](#credit-authorship-contribution-statement) Runco & Jaeger, 2012). Accordingly, ITS is understood as a cognitive trans- formation outcome that arises from learning processes rather than as a direct extension of technological knowledge. In contrast to AI literacy, which captures domain-specific technological competence, and self-directed learning, which governs how individuals regulate their learning processes, ITS emphasizes the transformation of knowledge and experience into creative, adaptive, and contextually relevant solutions. This distinction is critical to avoid conceptual redundancy, as ITS reflects the application and transformation of cognition, rather than knowledge acquisition (AI literacy) or learning regulation (SDL). By explicitly defining ITS as an outcome construct, this study ensures clear theoretical separation among the three constructs within the proposed process-based framework.

From a measurement perspective, ITS is operationalized through four key dimensions: (1) idea generation, defined as the ability to produce diverse and original ideas beyond conventional patterns ([Dou et al., 2021)](#credit-authorship-contribution-statement); (2) cognitive flexibility, referring to the capacity to shift perspectives and adapt problem-solving approaches ([Bobrowicz & Thibaut, 2023)](#credit-authorship-contribution-statement); (3) risk-taking attitude, indicating a will- ingness to experiment and view failure as an opportunity for learning ([Caliendo et al., 2009)](#credit-authorship-contribution-statement); and (4) problem reframing, which in- volves interpreting problems from alternative viewpoints to develop innovative solutions (Kim et al., 2020). These dimensions capture higher-order cognitive processes that are conceptually distinct from both technological competence and learning regulation mechanisms.

Within the proposed framework, ITS is expected to positively influence FinTech adoption capability. Individuals with stronger innovative thinking skills are more capable of identifying novel application opportunities, redesigning existing processes, and adapting technologies to meet specific contextual needs. Unlike perception-based technology adoption models that primarily emphasize atti- tudes such as perceived usefulness or ease of use, ITS reflects a deeper cognitive capability that enables individuals to actively shape how technologies are utilized and integrated into practice. This perspective aligns with a capability-based view of technology use, wherein effective adoption depends not only on users’ perceptions but also on their ability to creatively apply and adapt technological tools ([Cumming et al., 2023)](#credit-authorship-contribution-statement) Accordingly, ITS is positioned as a cognitive transformation outcome that mediates the relationship between learning processes and the development of practical technological capabilities within the proposed process-based model. Based on this theoretical rationale, the following hypothesis is formulated: 

**H6**. Innovative thinking skill has a positive effect on FinTech adoption capability.

### _2.5._ _FinTech adoption capability_

FinTech Adoption Capability (FAC) in this study is conceptualized as an individual's ability to effectively understand, utilize, and critically evaluate financial technologies (FinTech) in real-world contexts, rather than merely reflecting their intention or perception toward adoption. This definition adopts a capability-based perspective, emphasizing what individuals are able to do with technology in practice, rather than how they perceive it. In contemporary settings, FinTech encompasses a broad spectrum of digital financial services, including mobile banking, e-wallets, robo-advisory systems, blockchain-based applications, crowdfunding platforms, and online lending services (Tran et al., 2024; Wang, 2023). For finance students, FAC serves as a key indicator of their readiness to adapt to rapidly evolving financial technologies and to effectively select and apply appropriate FinTech tools in response to situational demands ([Bermeo-Giraldo et al., 2023)](#credit-authorship-contribution-statement). As FinTech becomes increasingly embedded in everyday digital life, individuals are required 

not only to use these technologies but also to understand their functionalities and broader implications in practical contexts. From a measurement perspective, FAC is operationalized through five key dimensions: (1) knowledge of FinTech tools, referring to users' understanding of currently available digital financial systems (Hurani & Abdel-Haq, 2025); (2) frequency of FinTech usage, indicating the extent to which individuals consistently engage with FinTech applications in everyday financial activities ([Bajunaied et al., 2023)](#credit-authorship-contribution-statement); (3) perceived ease of use, reflecting users' ability to understand and operate FinTech applications independently without external assistance (Wilson et al., 2021); (4) perceived usefulness, referring to the extent to which users recognize FinTech as enhancing convenience, efficiency, and access to financial services (Wilson et al., 2021); and (5) security and trust awareness, rep- resenting users' understanding of security features, data protection, and the reliability of FinTech platforms when making usage de- cisions (Jafri et al., 2024). These dimensions emphasize capability and informed judgment, rather than purely perception-based attitudes. By conceptualizing FAC as a capability-based outcome, this study departs from traditional technology adoption models that primarily focus on perceptions such as ease of use and usefulness. Instead, it highlights individuals’ practical ability to engage with and effectively apply FinTech technologies. This perspective is consistent with the proposed process-based framework, in which foundational knowledge, learning mechanisms, and cognitive transformation jointly contribute to the development of applied tech- nological capability. Based on the review of the relevant literature, a conceptual framework is developed to illustrate the hypothesized relationships among the study variables, as presented in [Fig. 1](#3-research-methodology) as follows.

## 3. Research methodology

### _3.1._ _Research design_

This study employs a quantitative research design to examine the causal relationships among AI literacy, self-directed learning, innovative thinking skills, and FinTech adoption capability. The target population comprises Generation Z finance students in the upper undergraduate years (e.g., third- and fourth-year students) at universities in Thailand. This group is theoretically appropriate, as these students are likely to have prior exposure to both financial education and digital financial technologies, enabling them to meaningfully evaluate and apply FinTech tools within academic and practical contexts. Data were collected באמצע ות an online survey distributed through digital channels commonly used by the target population, including email and social media platforms. To ensure consistency in respondents’ understanding and to minimize measurement ambiguity, the questionnaire included brief explanations of key constructs.

In the absence of a comprehensive national sampling frame, this study adopted a convenience sampling approach. While this

Therefore, the results should be interpreted within the context of finance students in Thailand, and caution is warranted when extending the findings to other populations. Additionally, the study does not explicitly account for vari- ations across institutional types, geographic regions, or socioeconomic backgrounds. These contextual factors may influence in- dividuals’ access to digital technologies and learning opportunities, potentially contributing to unobserved heterogeneity in the results. Future studies are encouraged to employ more diverse and stratified sampling strategies to enhance external validity. The minimum sample size was determined using Cochran's formula for an unknown population, which indicated a recommended sample of 384 respondents. The final dataset consists of 391 valid responses, exceeding this threshold and thereby supporting the application of Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). However, it is important to note that an adequate sample size does not guarantee representativeness. Accordingly, the findings should be interpreted within the scope of the sampled popu- lation. Overall, the research design is appropriate for examining the proposed theoretical relationships within a defined educational context, while acknowledging the inherent limitations associated with non-probability sampling.

### _3.2._ _Measurement instruments_

This study utilized a structured questionnaire as the primary instrument for collecting quantitative data. The measurement items were developed through an extensive review of prior literature related to the key constructs, namely AI literacy, self-directed learning, innovative thinking skills, and FinTech adoption capability. All items were carefully adapted to align with the context of Generation Z undergraduate finance students in Thailand, thereby ensuring both conceptual relevance and contextual appropriateness. The ques- tionnaire was organized into two main sections. The first section collected demographic information and background characteristics related to respondents' learning experiences and technology usage. The second section assessed the core constructs using a five-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). This scaling approach was intended to capture respondents’ self- perceived levels of capability, learning behaviors, and cognitive processes associated with each construct.

All constructs were specified as reflective measurement models, based on the assumption that the observed indicators represent manifestations of their respective latent variables. Accordingly, variations in the latent constructs are expected to be reflected in corresponding changes across their indicators, which are conceptually interchangeable within each construct. Prior to data collection, the questionnaire was subjected to a content validity assessment by subject-matter experts with expertise in finance, financial tech- nology, and artificial intelligence. A pilot study was subsequently conducted to evaluate the clarity and reliability of the measurement items.

To further enhance measurement quality, item validation procedures were implemented. During the measurement model evalu- ation stage, indicators with low factor loadings or insufficient contributions to construct reliability were critically assessed and, where necessary, removed in accordance with established thresholds in the PLS-SEM literature. This procedure ensured that only indicators demonstrating adequate reliability and validity were retained for subsequent analysis. In addition, nonresponse bias was examined during the data collection process to ensure the robustness of the dataset. Detailed information regarding the constructs, their di- mensions, operational definitions, and corresponding measurement items is presented in Table 1.

### _3.3._ _Data analysis methods_

Data analysis in this study commenced with descriptive statistics to summarize respondents' characteristics and to examine overall patterns across the key constructs, namely AI literacy, self-directed learning, innovative thinking skills, and FinTech adoption capa- bility. Measures such as means, standard deviations, and distributional properties were used to capture respondents’ self-reported capabilities, learning behaviors, and cognitive tendencies.

Prior to testing the structural relationships, the measurement model was evaluated in terms of reliability and validity. Internal consistency reliability was assessed using Cronbach's alpha and composite reliability (CR), while convergent validity was examined through the average variance extracted (AVE). Variance inflation factor (VIF) values were also analyzed to detect potential multi- collinearity among indicators. Given that the data were collected באמצעו ת a self-reported questionnaire, common method bias (CMB) was considered a potential concern. To mitigate this issue, the questionnaire was carefully designed with clear construct definitions and structured to minimize ambiguity in respondents' interpretations. In addition, statistical assessments were conducted to evaluate whether the observed relationships were unduly influenced by shared measurement methods rather than reflecting substantive as- sociations among constructs.

Following confirmation of the measurement model's adequacy, Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) was employed as the primary analytical technique for hypothesis testing. The use of PLS-SEM is justified for several reasons. First, the proposed framework involves multiple direct and indirect relationships, including sequential mediation effects, which require the simultaneous estimation of interdependent structural paths. Second, the study aims not only to test theoretical relationships but also to explain and predict the development of FinTech adoption capability within a capability-based process framework. Third, PLS-SEM is particularly suitable for exploratory and prediction-oriented models in which latent constructs are measured using multiple indicators, with an emphasis on maximizing the explained variance of endogenous variables.

The structural model was evaluated by examining path coefficients, t-statistics, and p-values to determine the significance of the hypothesized relationships. Additionally, coefficients of determination (R2 and adjusted R2) were reported to assess the model's explanatory power, while effect size measures (f2) were used to evaluate the relative contribution of each predictor. Indirect effects were also analyzed to test the mediating roles of self-directed learning and innovative thinking skills in the relationship between AI 

literacy and FinTech adoption capability. This analytical approach provides robust empirical evidence on how foundational techno- logical competence, learning regulation, and cognitive transformation jointly contribute to the development of FinTech adoption capability among Generation Z finance students in Thailand.

## 4. Results

This section presents the empirical results concerning the impact of AI literacy on FinTech adoption capability, along with the mediating roles of self-directed learning and innovative thinking skills among Generation Z finance students in Thailand. The findings are reported in a structured sequence, beginning with a description of respondents’ demographic characteristics, followed by the evaluation of the measurement and structural models, and concluding with the results of hypothesis testing and the analysis of indirect effects.

The final sample consisted of 391 Generation Z finance students. Female respondents constituted the majority of the sample (65.00%), while male respondents accounted for 35.00%. In terms of institutional affiliation, most participants were enrolled in public universities (83.40%), with the remaining 16.60% attending private institutions. Regarding internship experience, the largest pro- portion of respondents reported internship durations of less than three months (69.60%), followed by those with internships lasting 3–5 months and 6–8 months. Regarding to academic performance, the majority of students reported a cumulative grade point average (GPA) in the range of 3.01 to 3.50 (40.20%). This was followed by students with GPAs between 3.51 and 4.00, and those with GPAs between 2.51 and 3.00. A comprehensive summary of the respondents’ demographic characteristics is provided in [Table 2.](#4-results) The evaluation of the measurement model indicates that all latent constructs demonstrate satisfactory levels of reliability and convergent validity. As reported in Table 3, Cronbach's alpha values range from 0.758 to 0.884, exceeding the recommended threshold of 0.70 and indicating adequate internal consistency across all constructs. Similarly, Composite Reliability (CR) values are consistently above 0.70, further confirming the reliability of the measurement scales. With respect to convergent validity, the Average Variance Extracted (AVE) values for all constructs surpass the minimum threshold of 0.50, suggesting that the indicators adequately capture the variance of their respective latent variables. Taken together, these findings confirm that the measurement model satisfies established criteria for both reliability and convergent validity.

At the indicator level, most factor loadings fall within acceptable ranges, reflecting strong relationships between the indicators and their corresponding constructs. However, a small number of indicators exhibit relatively lower loadings (e.g., Ethical Consideration = 0.546 and AI Communication Skill = 0.686). According to established PLS-SEM guidelines, indicators with loadings between 0.40 and 

0.70 may be retained, provided that overall construct reliability and convergent validity remain satisfactory. In this study, all con- structs meet the recommended thresholds for CR and AVE, indicating that the inclusion of these indicators does not compromise the overall quality of the measurement model. Given that, these items were retained to preserve the theoretical completeness and con- ceptual breadth of the constructs. With respect to the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) values for all indicators are below the critical cut- off thresholds, indicating the absence of multicollinearity issues that could potentially bias the estimation results. Overall, these findings confirm that the measurement model is both reliable and valid, and therefore suitable for subsequent structural model evaluation and hypothesis testing.

Discriminant validity of the measurement model was assessed using both the Heterotrait–Monotrait Ratio of Correlations (HTMT) and the Fornell–Larcker criterion to ensure that each latent construct is empirically and conceptually distinct. The HTMT results show that all inter-construct correlation values fall below the recommended threshold of 0.85, indicating that the constructs are sufficiently differentiated and free from problematic overlap. Consistent with these findings, the Fornell–Larcker criterion further supports discriminant validity. Specifically, the square root of the Average Variance Extracted (AVE) for each construct—reported along the diagonal of the correlation matrix—exceeds its corresponding correlations with other constructs. This suggests that each latent var- iable explains the variance of its own indicators more effectively than that of other constructs. The evidence from both HTMT and Fornell–Larcker assessments confirms that the measurement model exhibits satisfactory discriminant validity. These results indicate

The structural model was evaluated using the coefficient of determination (R2), which indicates that the model exhibits satisfactory explanatory power across all endogenous constructs. Specifically, the R2 value for self-directed learning is 0.415, suggesting that AI literacy accounts for a moderate proportion of the variance in individuals' ability to regulate their own learning processes. To assess the predictive relevance of the model, Stone–Geisser's Q2 values were computed using the blindfolding procedure. These findings indicate that the proposed model not only explains the relationships observed within the sample but also demonstrates meaningful predictive capability in estimating key outcome variables in practical settings. Specifically, AI literacy has a significant and positive effect on self-directed learning (β = 0.644, p _\<_ 0.001), with a very large effect size (f2 = 0.710). This finding underscores the central role of AI-related knowledge in strengthening students' capacity to regulate and manage their own learning processes. From a practical standpoint, it suggests that enhancing students’ AI literacy can substantially improve their ability to engage in self-directed learning, which is critical for adapting to rapidly evolving digital and financial environments. In addition, AI literacy exerts significant positive effects on both innovative thinking skills (β = 0.241, p _\<_ 0.001) and FinTech adoption capability (β = 0.397, p _\<_ 0.001), with small to moderate effect sizes. These findings indicate that while AI literacy alone may not be sufficient to fully drive innovation or FinTech capability, it serves as a foundational enabler that facilitates more effective engagement with digital tools and technological systems in practice. Furthermore, self-directed learning demonstrates a strong and statistically significant positive effect on innovative thinking skills (β = 0.527, p _\<_ 0.001), accompanied by a large effect size (f2 = 0.325). This highlights the role of self-directed learning as a key behavioral mechanism that fosters higher-order cognitive development. In practical terms, students who actively regulate their own learning processes are more likely to develop cognitive flexibility and creative problem-solving abilities, which are essential in dy- namic financial and technological contexts. However, no significant direct relationship is found between self-directed learning and FinTech adoption capability (β = − 0.087, p = 0.196), with a negligible effect size. This result suggests that although self-directed learning is an important driver of cognitive development, it may not directly translate into effective FinTech usage unless it is com- plemented by higher-order cognitive capabilities, such as innovative thinking skills.

Finally, innovative thinking skills exhibit a significant positive effect on FinTech adoption capability (β = 0.383, p _\<_ 0.001), with a moderate effect size. This finding indicates that innovative thinking serves as a critical mechanism through which knowledge and learning processes are translated into effective FinTech adoption. From a practical perspective, it emphasizes the importance of cultivating creative and adaptive thinking skills among students to enhance their ability to apply FinTech solutions in real-world financial contexts. The results of the indirect effects and mediation analysis provide robust evidence of the underlying relational mechanisms among the constructs in the proposed model. Specifically, AI literacy exerts a significant positive indirect effect on innovative thinking skills

through the mediating role of self-directed learning (β = 0.340, p _\<_ 0.001). This finding indicates that AI-related knowledge enhances students’ capacity for self-directed learning, which in turn facilitates the development of higher-order innovative thinking skills. However, no significant indirect effect of AI literacy on FinTech adoption capability through self-directed learning alone is observed (β = − 0.056, p = 0.204), which is consistent with the previously identified non-significant direct relationship between these variables. In contrast, AI literacy demonstrates a significant positive indirect effect on FinTech adoption capability via innovative thinking skills (β = 0.092, p _\<_ 0.001), highlighting the critical role of innovative thinking as a cognitive mechanism through which AI literacy is translated into effective FinTech adoption.

Moreover, self-directed learning exhibits a significant indirect effect on FinTech adoption capability through innovative thinking skills (β = 0.202, p _\<_ 0.001). This result suggests that the influence of self-directed learning on FinTech adoption operates through its capacity to foster higher-order cognitive processes, rather than exerting a direct behavioral effect. In other words, self-directed learning must first be transformed into innovative thinking before it can meaningfully contribute to FinTech usage capability. The serial mediation analysis further reveals that AI literacy has a significant indirect effect on FinTech adoption capability through the sequential mediating roles of self-directed learning and innovative thinking skills (β = 0.130, p _\<_ 0.001). This finding supports a process-based mechanism in which AI literacy enhances self-directed learning, which subsequently cultivates innovative thinking skills that ultimately lead to more effective and sustainable FinTech adoption. ## 5. Discussion

The findings of this study provide strong empirical support for the proposed process-based framework by highlighting the role of AI literacy in strengthening FinTech adoption capability through the sequential mechanisms of self-directed learning and innovative thinking skills. Rather than introducing an entirely new theoretical paradigm, the results demonstrate how established theoretical perspectives can be integrated to explain a structured developmental pathway from knowledge to capability. First, AI literacy exerts a strong positive effect on self-directed learning, indicating that students with higher levels of AI-related knowledge are more likely to actively regulate and manage their own learning processes. This finding is consistent with prior research (Long & Magerko, 2020; Walter, 2024), which conceptualizes AI literacy as encompassing not only technical knowledge but also critical evaluation and ethical awareness. From a theoretical standpoint, this result reinforces the view that knowledge serves as a catalyst for self-regulated learning behaviors (Garrison, 1997a, 1997b; Knowles, 1975). In this sense, AI literacy can be understood as a foundational enabler that fosters deeper engagement in learning processes, rather than directly determining behavioral outcomes. Moreover, AI literacy shows significant direct effects on both innovative thinking skills and FinTech adoption capability, although the magnitude of these relationships is relatively small to moderate. This suggests that while AI literacy provides important cognitive resources, it is not sufficient on its own to fully explain the development of applied technological capability. This finding aligns with prior studies emphasizing that knowledge alone does not necessarily lead to effective technology use, particularly in complex domains such as finance ([Broekhuizen et al., 2023;](#credit-authorship-contribution-statement) Pinski & Benlian, 2024). At the same time, it challenges perspectives that treat technological knowledge as the principal determinant of adoption behavior, thereby underscoring the importance of additional mediating mechanisms.

In relation to self-directed learning, the results indicate a significant positive effect on innovative thinking skills, thereby supporting prior research linking self-regulated learning to cognitive flexibility and creative problem-solving (Morris & Rohs, 2021; Tekkol & Demirel, 2018). However, contrary to the initial hypothesis, self-directed learning does not have a significant direct effect on FinTech adoption capability. This unexpected result suggests that self-directed learning alone may be insufficient to translate learning efforts into effective technology use, particularly in contexts involving complex decision-making and risk evaluation. One plausible expla- nation is that self-directed learning primarily enhances the processes of knowledge acquisition and regulation, but does not directly influence the practical application of knowledge unless that knowledge is transformed into higher-order cognitive capabilities. This interpretation is consistent with prior research suggesting that learning processes must be cognitively internalized and restructured before they can shape behavioral outcomes (Rashid & Asghar, 2016). It also offers an alternative perspective to studies reporting a direct association between self-directed learning and technology adoption, suggesting that such a relationship may depend on

The mediation and serial mediation analyses further strengthen these interpretations by showing that innovative thinking skills function as a critical intermediary mechanism linking both AI literacy and self-directed learning to FinTech adoption capability. This finding suggests that the primary contribution of the study lies in clarifying the process through which knowledge and learning be- haviors are translated into applied technological capability. More specifically, the results indicate that self-directed learning con- tributes to FinTech adoption only when it fosters innovative thinking. This is in line with arguments advanced by [Cumming et al. (2023)](#credit-authorship-contribution-statement) and Maple et al. (2023), who emphasize that effective technology adoption in dynamic environments depends not merely on possessing knowledge, but on the ability to interpret and apply that knowledge creatively. The overall findings support a process-oriented perspective in which AI literacy functions as an input capability, self-directed learning operates as a learning mechanism, and innovative thinking skills represent a cognitive transformation process that ultimately leads to FinTech adoption capability. By emphasizing this structured pathway, the study provides a more nuanced explanation of how technological capability develops, moving beyond perception-based or technology-centered models toward a more integrative and process-based under- standing. Moreover, the focus on Generation Z is theoretically well justified within this framework, as this cohort is characterized by extensive exposure to digital technologies, adaptive learning behaviors, and a strong tendency toward autonomous and technology-integrated decision-making. These characteristics make Generation Z a particularly appropriate context for examining how AI literacy, learning processes, and cognitive transformation jointly contribute to the development of technological capability.

### _5.1._ _Transforming knowledge into practical application in the digital finance era of the younger generation_

The findings of this study indicate that the development of FinTech adoption capability among Generation Z finance students is not determined solely by technological knowledge, but rather by the ability to translate that knowledge into effective decision-making and problem-solving in real-world contexts. In contemporary digital financial environments, students with higher levels of AI literacy are better positioned to understand technological systems and evaluate associated risks. However, the effective application of such knowledge requires more than technical understanding; it depends on individuals’ capacity to regulate their learning processes and transform insights into actionable strategies.

Self-directed learning plays a critical role in enabling individuals to continuously acquire, update, and refine their knowledge, particularly in rapidly evolving technological contexts. Nevertheless, the findings demonstrate that self-directed learning alone does not directly lead to FinTech adoption capability unless it is complemented by higher-order cognitive abilities. This underscores the pivotal role of innovative thinking as a mechanism that bridges the gap between knowledge acquisition and practical application. Innovative thinking skills enable individuals to reinterpret problems, explore alternative solutions, and creatively apply technological tools to achieve desired outcomes.

These results reinforce a process-oriented perspective, suggesting that effective FinTech adoption is not driven solely by knowledge or learning effort, but by the transformation of these elements into adaptive, context-sensitive decision-making capabilities. From a broader standpoint, the findings reflect an evolving role of younger generations in digital societies. Rather than functioning as passive users of technology, Generation Z individuals are increasingly expected to act as active decision-makers who critically evaluate, adapt, and apply FinTech solutions in dynamic environments. These insights highlight the importance of fostering not only technological literacy but also learning and higher-order cognitive capabilities in order to better prepare students for real-world financial decision- making.

### _5.2._ _Implications of the study_

The findings of this study contribute to the management education literature by demonstrating that the development of technology- related capability is not merely a function of technical knowledge acquisition, but rather the result of a structured learning process involving self-regulation and cognitive transformation. This perspective is consistent with contemporary approaches in management education that emphasize experiential learning, capability development, and the integration of higher-order thinking skills in pre- paring students for complex and dynamic environments. From a theoretical standpoint, the results extend prior research by showing that AI literacy operates as a foundational capability that must be transformed through learning processes and innovative cognition before it can meaningfully influence practical technology use. This underscores the need to reposition technology education within management programs from a content-driven orientation toward a process-based learning framework that integrates knowledge acquisition, learning behavior, and cognitive skill development.

From a curriculum design perspective, the findings suggest that finance and business education programs should move beyond isolated courses on AI or FinTech tools and instead adopt a more integrated and interdisciplinary curriculum structure. In particular, AI literacy should be embedded across multiple courses and reinforced through learning activities designed to cultivate self-directed learning and innovative thinking skills. For instance, curricula may incorporate scaffolded tasks that require students to indepen- dently explore AI applications, critically assess FinTech solutions, and iteratively refine their approaches through reflection and feedback.

In terms of pedagogy, the results indicate a shift away from passive knowledge transmission toward more active and practice- oriented learning strategies. Instructional approaches such as project-based learning, problem-based learning, financial simulations, and case-based analysis can be systematically designed to foster experimentation, critical evaluation, and creative problem-solving in real-world contexts. These methods enable students to apply AI and FinTech knowledge in complex scenarios, thereby facilitating the transformation of theoretical understanding into practical capability.

Furthermore, assessment practices should be aligned with this process-oriented perspective. Rather than emphasizing knowledge recall alone, evaluation methods should focus on students’ ability to apply, adapt, and innovate in response to real-world financial challenges. This may include tasks such as designing FinTech solutions, analyzing digital financial risks, or developing data-driven decision-making strategies. Such an approach to assessment more effectively captures the development of applied competencies required in the digital economy. The findings suggest that preparing future finance professionals for the digital era requires an in- tegrated educational approach that simultaneously fosters AI literacy, self-directed learning, and innovative thinking skills. This approach not only equips students with the knowledge necessary to understand emerging technologies, but also enables them to apply these technologies effectively in dynamic and uncertain financial environments.

### _5.3._ _Limitations and future research directions_

Despite providing meaningful insights into the role of AI literacy in shaping FinTech adoption capability through the mediating mechanisms of self-directed learning and innovative thinking skills, several limitations should be considered when interpreting the findings of this study. First, the research is based on cross-sectional data collected at a single point in time, which restricts the ability to capture developmental changes and long-term dynamics in learning processes and FinTech usage behavior. Although the proposed relationships are theoretically grounded, causal interpretations should therefore be approached with caution. Second, the sample is limited to Generation Z finance students in Thailand, a group influenced by specific educational, techno- logical, and socio-cultural contexts. This context-specific focus may constrain the generalizability of the findings to other populations, such as students from different academic disciplines, financial industry professionals, or individuals in countries with varying levels of technological advancement and economic development. Moreover, the use of convenience sampling, combined with the absence of differentiation across institutional types, geographic regions, and socioeconomic backgrounds, may further affect the representa- tiveness of the sample. These limitations should be carefully considered when assessing the broader applicability of the proposed model.

Third, the study relies on self-reported questionnaire data, which may introduce perceptual and self-assessment biases. Although efforts were made to enhance clarity and reduce ambiguity in the measurement design, such biases may still influence the accuracy of the responses and should be acknowledged when interpreting the results.

Future research can address these limitations in several ways. Longitudinal research designs would provide deeper insights into how AI literacy, self-directed learning, innovative thinking skills, and FinTech adoption capability evolve over time, thereby strengthening causal inference. Expanding the sample to include participants from diverse academic disciplines, professional back- grounds, and geographic contexts would enhance external validity and improve the generalizability of the findings. Additionally, future studies may incorporate additional variables—such as risk perception, trust in digital financial systems, or prior experience with FinTech usage—to develop a more comprehensive understanding of technology adoption behavior. Such extensions would contribute to a more nuanced perspective on how technological, cognitive, and contextual factors jointly shape FinTech adoption in the digital economy.

## 6. Conclusion

This study set out to examine the influence of AI literacy on FinTech adoption capability by incorporating the mediating roles of self-directed learning and innovative thinking skills among Generation Z finance students in Thailand. The findings demonstrate that AI literacy serves as a foundational capability that significantly enhances self-directed learning, innovative thinking skills, and FinTech adoption capability. Importantly, the results indicate that technological capability does not emerge from knowledge alone, but rather from a structured process in which learning behaviors and cognitive transformation play central roles.

Specifically, self-directed learning and innovative thinking skills operate as sequential mechanisms that translate AI-related knowledge into effective FinTech usage. While self-directed learning does not exert a direct effect on FinTech adoption capability, it contributes indirectly through innovative thinking skills, underscoring the critical role of cognitive transformation in bridging knowledge and practical application. These findings support a process-oriented perspective of technology capability development, highlighting the need to develop AI literacy, learning processes, and innovative cognition in an integrated manner. From a theoretical perspective, this study extends the existing literature by moving beyond perception-based and technology- centric explanations of FinTech adoption toward a more comprehensive, capability-oriented framework. From a practical stand- point, the findings suggest that developing competencies in the digital economy requires more than technical training alone. 

Educational strategies should simultaneously foster AI literacy, self-directed learning, and innovative thinking skills to enable students to effectively adapt to rapidly evolving financial technologies. These insights provide valuable implications for curriculum design, educational policy, and instructional practices aimed at preparing future finance professionals to navigate the complexities of the digital financial landscape.
